issues.description: The introduction explicitly states that the interventions will be placed BEFORE the collaborative recall phase ('before exposing participants to misinformation'), with a rationale about inoculating participants before misinformation takes effect. However, the procedure section (Section 2.5) clearly describes the opposite order: (1) movie, (2) collaborative recall, (3) interventions, (4) individual memory test. The interventions come AFTER misinformation exposure. This is a fundamental contradiction that affects the entire theoretical rationale, since the IMP-based justification (destroying the consistency assumption before misinformation is introduced) would require pre-misinformation placement. This also undermines the explicit analogy to Sagarin et al.'s (2002) inoculation approach.
issues.quote: What is important, we decided to place the methods inducing resistance to misinformation before the collaborative recall phase (that is, before exposing participants to misinformation). The main reason for that is that we wanted to inoculate participants against the influence of misinformation before it could take effect.

issues.description: The design section states that 'discussed and non-discussed items will be fully counterbalanced,' which would mean that the assignment of which critical details are discussed vs. not discussed varies systematically across pairs. However, the procedure section explicitly states that all pairs discuss the same four critical details. If every pair discusses the same set of items, there is no counterbalancing whatsoever; the discussed vs. non-discussed comparison is completely confounded with item content. This means any observed difference could be due to intrinsic difficulty differences between the always-discussed and never-discussed items rather than the effect of misinformation.
issues.quote: In order to ensure sufficient discussion, each pair will discuss the same set of four critical details during the collaborative recall phase. For example, all pairs will talk about Eric's cap color and his company logo.

issues.description: The procedure section consistently describes the individual memory test as containing 20 open-ended questions and derives four indices from this open-ended format (correct answers, misinformation-consistent answers, other answers, overall answers). However, the analysis plan section states 'the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format,' which directly contradicts the open-ended format. These are fundamentally different test formats with different scoring systems, chance performance rates, and susceptibility to response bias. It is unclear which format will actually be used.
issues.quote: In the present research, the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format.

issues.subcategory: no manipulation check for MORI technique
issues.description: There is no mention of checking whether participants detected that they were watching different movie versions. If participants become aware of the deception, the entire basis for the memory conformity paradigm is undermined. Standard practice in MORI studies (e.g., Garry et al., 2008) includes a post-experimental check asking participants whether they noticed anything unusual about the movie or suspected they watched different versions. The exclusion criteria only mention 'technical problems' and do not address awareness of the manipulation.
issues.quote: We will exclude participants in the case of any technical problems during the experimental session.

issues.description: The entire theoretical framework hinges on the distinction between participants who are aware of discrepancies between their own memories and the co-witness's information versus those who are not. The authors repeatedly emphasize that their methods should be effective primarily for 'aware' participants. However, there is no measure or procedure described for assessing participants' awareness of discrepancies. Without this measurement, the central theoretical prediction cannot be tested, and the mechanism cannot be evaluated.
issues.quote: our methods of reducing the memory conformity effect are directed towards the participants who are aware of the discrepancy between both the original information and the misinformation obtained from the partner

issues.description: The authors combine effect sizes from only two studies (g = 1.92 and g = 0.38) using random-effects meta-analysis to estimate a joint effect size of 1.13. With only two studies, the between-study heterogeneity variance (tau-squared) is estimated with essentially zero precision. The resulting pooled estimate is highly unreliable, and the confidence interval around it would be extremely wide. The five-fold difference between the two effect sizes (1.92 vs. 0.38) further underscores the instability. Basing the power analysis on this unreliable pooled estimate is problematic.
issues.quote: The existing results as regards effect sizes are Hedges' g = 1.92, N = 55 (Ito et al., 2019) and Hedges' g = 0.38, N = 74 (Kękuś et al., 2020)... random effects were assumed while calculating the joint effect size, which was 1.13.

issues.description: The correlation of r = 0.07 between repeated measures (discussed vs. non-discussed items) used in the power analysis is extremely low. In most within-subjects designs, correlations between conditions are substantially higher (typically 0.30–0.70). A correlation this low suggests the within-subjects design provides virtually no advantage over a between-subjects design. This value may be an artifact of the small samples from which it was derived, or it may reflect a coding or computational error. If the true correlation is higher, the study would need fewer participants; if it's genuinely this low, it raises questions about whether discussed and non-discussed items are measuring the same underlying construct.
issues.quote: The joint correlation of results in the discussed and non-discussed items in both studies available was 0.07.

issues.subcategory: multiple dependent variables without primary outcome
issues.description: The study collects multiple dependent variables (correct answers, misinformation-consistent answers, other answers, total answers, and certainty ratings on a 0-100% scale) but does not designate a primary outcome measure. The analysis plan states they will 'explore the individual memory test's scores for the critical details using analysis of variance (ANOVA), using all four indices.' Without specifying which outcome is primary, there are undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom that inflate the risk of Type I error.
issues.quote: We will explore the individual memory test's scores for the critical details using analysis of variance (ANOVA), using all four indices: the number of correct answers, number of answers consistent with misinformation, other answers, and the overall number of answers.

issues.description: The analysis plan describes follow-up pairwise comparisons between all groups if the omnibus interaction is significant, but no correction for multiple comparisons is mentioned. With four groups, there are six possible pairwise comparisons. Using directional tests without correction substantially inflates the family-wise error rate. The power analysis also does not account for any correction.
issues.quote: In the case of a significant main interaction, follow-up comparisons between pairs of groups will be performed... Comparisons among all groups and directional significance tests are assumed.

issues.description: The control group listens to a podcast about 'soft skills related to social attitudes,' while the experimental groups receive interventions of varying types (podcasts about memory, DRM task + feedback + podcast). The Demonstration and motivation condition involves substantially different activities (word list memorization, written recall, personalized feedback, plus a podcast) compared to both the podcast-only conditions and the control. This creates differential cognitive engagement, task novelty, and time-on-task confounds. Any differences could be attributed to these non-specific factors rather than the specific content of the interventions.
issues.quote: In the control group, participants will listen to a podcast concerning soft skills related to social attitudes.

issues.subcategory: DRM as demonstration of memory conformity vulnerability
issues.description: The DRM paradigm demonstrates susceptibility to associative false memories (falsely remembering semantically related words), which is a fundamentally different memory phenomenon from memory conformity (incorporating information from a co-witness). Demonstrating vulnerability to one type of memory error does not necessarily demonstrate vulnerability to another. The theoretical leap from 'your memory produced a word that wasn't on the list' to 'your memory may incorporate information from your discussion partner' is not well justified. Participants may not perceive these as related phenomena.
issues.quote: directly demonstrating the fallibility of memory to the participants... a substantially shortened and simplified procedure based on the DRM paradigm will be used

issues.subcategory: missing inter-rater reliability plan for open-ended scoring
issues.description: The individual memory test uses open-ended questions that must be scored and categorized into multiple categories (correct, misinformation-consistent, other). This requires subjective judgment, especially for ambiguous responses. No inter-rater reliability plan, coding scheme, or blinding of coders to condition is described. Without these, the scoring of the primary dependent variable is vulnerable to experimenter bias and unreliable classification.
issues.quote: The test will contain 20 open-ended questions... Four indices will be derived from the open-ended test

issues.description: There is no mention of blinding the experimenter to condition. The experimenter administers different interventions to different groups and is thus necessarily aware of condition assignment. Since the experimenter also administers the individual memory test and presumably scores open-ended responses, demand characteristics and experimenter expectancy effects are possible. No procedures to mitigate this are described.

The analysis plan states that ALL discussed items will be categorized as containing misinformation, but simultaneously acknowledges that partners sometimes provide answers consistent with what the participant saw (e.g., through guessing). This means some items scored as 'misinformation-exposed' may not actually contain misinformation, adding noise and biasing the effect estimate toward zero. Despite acknowledging this, the authors do not plan to use the audio recordings of discussions to verify actual misinformation exposure on an item-by-item basis.
issues.quote: we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation, as the collaborative recall procedure is designed to expose participants to their partner's differing version of events.

issues.subcategory: normative influence not completely ruled out
issues.description: The authors claim that normative influence is 'completely ruled out' because participants complete the individual memory test alone. However, normative influence can persist through internalized social pressure: participants may have already adopted their partner's answer during discussion to avoid disagreement, and this adopted response may carry forward to the individual test. The mere absence of the partner during testing does not eliminate the influence of prior social dynamics. Furthermore, participants know their responses are being recorded, which introduces a residual evaluative context.
issues.quote: we assumed that the normative impact explanation of the memory conformity effect is completely ruled out in this study: participants work on their own and do not compare their answers with anybody

issues.description: The DRM procedure used in the Demonstration and motivation condition lacks essential details needed for replication: the total number of word lists, the number of words per list, presentation rate, modality (auditory vs. visual), which specific lists will be used (only one example is given), and the criteria for selecting the four lists that 'produce the strongest effect.' The mention of prior research guiding list selection is vague and unreferenced.
issues.quote: Four lists will be chosen which on the basis of our previous research with this procedure, produce the strongest effect.

issues.subcategory: no analysis plan for certainty ratings
issues.description: Participants provide subjective certainty ratings (0-100%) for each answer, but no analysis plan for these data is described. These ratings are potentially important for testing the theoretical framework (e.g., whether interventions increase confidence in own memories), yet they are collected without any stated analytical purpose.
issues.quote: for each question, the participants will be asked to rate the subjective certainty of each answer on a scale from 0% (complete uncertainty, guessing) to 100% (absolute certainty)

issues.subcategory: no plan for audio recording analysis
issues.description: The collaborative discussion is audio recorded, but there is no analysis plan for these recordings. The recordings could provide crucial data about whether misinformation was actually exchanged, the dynamics of the discussion (e.g., who yielded to whom), and whether participants expressed awareness of discrepancies. Without analyzing these recordings, key information about the manipulation's success is lost.
issues.quote: The discussion will be audio recorded.

issues.description: The authors acknowledge overlap between the three interventions (e.g., memory education content appears in both Education about memory and Demonstration and motivation), but do not design the study to control for or measure this overlap. The Extended warning includes information about the misinformation effect and source monitoring, which overlaps with Education about memory content. This makes it impossible to attribute differential effects to the unique components of each intervention.
issues.quote: we are aware of some overlap between the three interventions, for instance, teaching about memory is included is present in a way in both Education about memory and Demonstration and motivation.

issues.description: There is no plan for handling missing data, incomplete sessions, or cases where participants fail to answer some questions. With pairs of participants, if one member of a pair must be excluded, it is unclear what happens to their partner's data. No intention-to-treat vs. per-protocol analysis distinction is made.

issues.subcategory: no plan for disagreement during discussion
issues.description: The procedure mentions that if participants cannot reach agreement during collaborative recall, both responses will be documented, but the analysis plan does not specify how these cases will be handled. Non-agreement cases represent a different exposure condition (weaker misinformation) and could differentially affect the results.
issues.quote: If the participants are unable to reach an agreement, both responses will be documented.

issues.description: The study uses a silent movie about an electrician stealing objects, which has limited ecological validity compared to real crime witnessing (which involves emotional arousal, personal threat, auditory information, etc.). The discussion occurs in a structured format with PowerPoint-displayed questions, unlike natural co-witness conversations. The age restriction (16-35) and recruitment via internet/media advertisements further limit generalizability. These limitations are not discussed.
issues.quote: The participants enrolled in the study will be 16–35 years old; they will be invited to participate via advertisements in the media and on the internet.

issues.description: The Extended warning and Education about memory are each approximately 7-minute podcasts, but the Demonstration and motivation condition involves a DRM procedure (list presentation, written recall, feedback) plus a podcast, which likely takes substantially longer and involves active participation rather than passive listening. Duration and engagement level are not matched across conditions, creating potential confounds.
issues.quote: The extended warning will take the form of an approximately 7-minute podcast... The training will take the form of an approximately 7-minute podcast... a substantially shortened and simplified procedure based on the DRM paradigm will be used... Afterwards, the participants will be motivated to resist illegitimate influences.

issues.description: The manuscript states that pairs will be 'randomly assigned' to one of four groups but provides no details about the randomization procedure (simple randomization, block randomization, stratification, etc.), who generates the random sequence, or when assignment occurs (before or after the collaborative recall phase).
issues.quote: Pairs of participants will be randomly assigned to one of four groups

issues.description: The prediction that Demonstration and motivation will be most effective, followed by Extended warning, followed by Education about memory is presented as a hypothesis but lacks rigorous justification. The ranking is based on loose analogies to Sagarin et al.'s (2002) persuasion work and the general observation that warnings have produced inconsistent results, which does not provide a principled basis for predicting specific ordering among three novel interventions in a different domain.
issues.quote: Based on the research of Sagarin et al. (2002), we tentatively assume that the most effective technique in reducing the memory conformity effect will be Demonstration and motivation... the Extended warning against misinformation is expected to be slightly less effective than Demonstration and motivation but more effective than Education about memory.

issues.description: The IMP framework (Blank, 1998) was developed for the classic misinformation paradigm where post-event information is delivered impersonally. The authors acknowledge this but argue 'similar processes may apply' to memory conformity without providing evidence or detailed theoretical argument for why socially delivered misinformation (which involves interpersonal dynamics, credibility assessment, and social pressure) would follow the same framework. The social dimension of memory conformity may invoke processes not captured by IMP.
issues.quote: The IMP was developed in the context of the classic misinformation paradigm, in which the post-event information is delivered impersonally. However, similar processes may apply to the memory conformity paradigm.

issues.description: The Extended warning podcast includes specific information about the deception ('enlightenment'), while the Education about memory podcast does not appear to include this element. This means the Extended warning condition includes both general memory information AND specific revelation of deception, confounding these two elements. The specific content and scripts of the podcasts are not provided or appended, making it impossible to evaluate the actual distinctiveness and content validity of the interventions.
issues.quote: In addition, the podcast will explain why the deception was applied.

issues.subcategory: demand characteristics from hypothesis awareness probe
issues.description: Asking participants what they think the real purpose of the study was occurs after the individual memory test, so it cannot affect test performance. However, the analysis plan only describes this as 'exploratory' without specifying how hypothesis-aware participants will be treated (excluded, analyzed separately, etc.). More importantly, the interventions themselves (especially Extended warning, which includes enlightenment about the deception) explicitly reveal the study's purpose, creating strong demand characteristics in that condition.
issues.quote: Next, the subjects will be requested to say what they think the real purpose of the study was. Their responses will be recorded for exploratory analysis of any relationship between hypothesis awareness and performance.

issues.description: The filler tasks (logic puzzles for 15 minutes and multiplication problems for 5 minutes) are not described in sufficient detail for replication. The difficulty level, number of items, and whether performance is recorded are not mentioned. Filler task characteristics could differentially affect cognitive fatigue across conditions.
issues.quote: the participants will be engaged in a filler task (solving logic puzzles) for 15 minutes... the participants will be asked to work on multiplication problems for five minutes.

issues.description: Since participants are tested in pairs and provide mutual misinformation, their individual memory test scores are not independent. One participant's discussion behavior directly influences their partner's misinformation exposure. The analysis plan describes standard ANOVA without any mention of accounting for this paired dependency (e.g., through multilevel modeling or treating the pair as the unit of analysis).
issues.quote: Technically, a repeated-measures ANOVA will be used to analyze the data.

issues.description: The power analysis describes 240 participants in four groups (presumably 60 per group), but the power analysis for planned pairwise comparisons states the required sample size for medium effects is 82 participants. Pairwise comparisons between two groups of 60 each would involve 120 participants total, which exceeds 82. However, if the paired dependency of data is accounted for (pairs as unit of analysis), the effective sample size is halved to 30 per group (60 per comparison), which falls below the 82 threshold for medium effects.
issues.quote: For the planned comparisons between two groups, which will be necessary if the general interaction is significant, the required sample sizes are 492, 82, and 34 participants, respectively.
